https://www.dw.com/en/syria-arms-depot-e.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5MKOo The large explosion led to secondary explosions and fires that it took several hours to control Image: Moawia Atrash/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement Syrian authorities reported that at least 14 people were killed and another 11 wounded on Wednesday as a result of an explosion at a temporary site used to store weapons and remnants of the country's long-running civil war. The explosion took place near the city of Sarmada in the northwestern Idlib province. Emergency services and Red Cross workers rushed to locate and if possible rescue victims potentially trapped beneath the rubble Image: Moawia Atrash/dpa/picture alliance What do we know about the explosion? Syria's Defense Ministry said the weapons and war remnants were being stored termporarily at the site before being transported elsewhere. It said that some of its personnel were among those wounded. The explosion in an area full of volatile materials led to secondary explosions and fires that hampered the emergency response. Smoke billowed from the blast site for some time on Wednesday. "The toll from the explosion in a temporary storage for collecting weapons and war remnants near the city of Sarmada ... registered 14 killed and 11 injured in a preliminary count," the Idlib health department said. Firefigthers battled to bring the primary and secondary fires under control Image: Kasim Yusuf/Anadolu/picture alliance Authorities have not yet said what caused the explosion. It was the second fatal incident of its kind in Idlib province this month. On September 1, five people were killed and others were wounded when a vehicle carrying ammunition exploded in Binnish. Syria only recently emerged from more than a decade of civil war, when forces loyal to new President Ahmed al-Sharaa ousted Bashar Assad and took control of Damascus. Idlib was one of the hardest-hit regions in the country during the war. Idlib province is still awash with ordnance after fierce fighting from 2011 until late 2024 Image: Kasim Yusuf/Anadolu/picture alliance If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google , so you'll always see our verified news first. Photograph: Fabrice Coffrini/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the WHO’s director general, said he wanted clarification from the Russian government following unconfirmed reports of ‘a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause’. Photograph: Fabrice Coffrini/AFP/Getty Images World Health Organization WHO says it does not have ‘full picture’ from Russia following suspected plague death ‘Transparent information sharing’ from Moscow is required to conduct full risk assessment, UN agency says Luke Harding Senior international correspondent Wed 7 Oct 2026 16.46 EDT Last modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 17.22 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The World Health Organization has said it does not have the “full picture” from Russia following the suspected death from plague last week of a 28-year-old laboratory worker in Siberia. Darya Shipilova died two days after falling ill with cold-like symptoms . She was an employee at the anti-plague research institute in the eastern city of Irkutsk, with some reports suggesting she was infected after a workplace accident. The Russian authorities have denied a connection with the institute and say Shipilova died from “pneumonia of an unknown aetiology” . They insist there is no danger of a plague outbreak and have described the “sanitary and epidemiological” situation in the region as stable. At the same time, officials have imposed sweeping quarantine restrictions at the lab where Shipilova worked and in nearby hospitals. Staff were locked down inside the institute for three days, sleeping on the floors and on chairs, while tests were conducted. What do we know about death of anti-plague institute worker in Russia and is there a wider risk? Read more On Wednesday the WHO director general, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, said: “We don’t yet have the full picture of this event and we’re not able to conduct a full risk assessment. “Timely, complete and transparent information sharing is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public risks.” Tedros said he also wanted more clarification from the Russian government following unconfirmed media reports of “a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause”. “We assess any reporting from the community,” he said. “We asked Russia to respond to that. We’re waiting for an answer.” The WHO’s director of epidemic and pandemic management, Maria Van Kerkhove, said the agency still did not know how Shipilova became infected in the first place – and with what viral disease. If pneumonic plague was ruled out, “what did she actually die from?” Kerkhove asked. In an interview with local media , Shipilova’s 64-year-old mother, Svetlana, discounted the theory that her daughter had been infected after smashing a test tube. “I know the truth. I’m fending off stupid friends who believe this. A test tube is unbreakable, even if you throw it against the wall,” she said. She described her daughter as a dedicated worker and “pure person” devoted to her job. Former classmates are also sceptical she was infected at her workplace. One reportedly said: “They’ve smeared a woman without properly investigating. Knowing how hard-working and responsible she was, it just doesn’t add up for me.” The Kremlin has sought to downplay the incident and has brushed aside an offer of assistance made earlier this week by Donald Trump, the US president. The White House has pressed Moscow for more details of the case, while stressing the risk to the US is very low. On Tuesday Trump said he would speak about the plague issue “very soon” with Vladimir Putin, who celebrated his 74th birthday on Wednesday. The Kremlin said no call had been arranged but could be quickly organised. According to the Baikal Medical Journal , health officials in Irkutsk have taken extensive measures to stop a potential outbreak from spreading. Neighbours said workers in white protective suits and gas masks disinfected the two-storey brick building where Shipilova lived several times after her death last Friday. “The smell was unbearable and very pungent,” a woman in her 40s said. “A woman knocked on our door. I said: ‘What are you treating here?’ I already knew about the plague rumours. “She said: ‘It’s for cockroaches.’ But we don’t even have any cockroaches in our building. I saw her packing her overalls into a bag. I was like, ‘Well, I get it.’” Explore more on these topics World Health Organization Russia Europe Bubonic plague Infectious diseases news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.dw.com/en/hungary-s-parliame.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OC2M Orban's government had gradually curbed LGBTQ+ rights Image: Anna Szilagyi/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement Hungary's parliament on Tuesday passed a bill amending a 2021 law targeting the LGBTQ+ community that was passed under nationalist ex-leader Viktor Orban . The 2021 "child protection" law introduced restrictions on the "portrayal" or "promotion" of sexual and gender diversity in content accessible to children. In reality, this meant that even books addressing these topics in an age-appropriate manner could only be sold in black plastic packaging with warnings. Critics argued that the law promoted the bigoted view automatically linking homosexuality and child abuse. The European Court of Justice had also ruled in April that it violated EU treaties. Tuesday's amendment repeals most of the statute, except the provision protecting under-18s from sexually explicit or violent material. It passed with the support of the governing majority, with 139 lawmakers voting in favor and 51 against. Will Hungary's new govt. bring real change on LGBTQ+ rights? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video What brought about this change? Hungary's longtime Prime Minister Viktor Orban was voted out of office in April. While his successor Peter Magyar is also a conservative and an immigration hardliner, he promised to break with Orban's repressive policies on media, the judiciary, and other issues. Magyar has promised to dismantle what he calls the rampant corruption and authoritarian structures put in place under Orban's government. "We welcome this important signal of commitment for our common values," EU commissioners Michael McGrath and Hadja Lahbib said in a joint statement. The bloc then unfroze €4.2 billion ($4.7 billion) in funding to Hungary following the vote.
